name: dependency-injection
intent: Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container.
problem: An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.
context: Applies whenever a component's collaborators are chosen per deployment, per environment or per test, whenever constructing them is expensive or platform-specific, and whenever a framework owns object creation (request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI screens, message consumers). It matters most in large object graphs where one abstraction has several implementations and lifetimes must be managed (singleton, request-scoped, transient); it is unnecessary when the collaborators are pure values or when construction is a private detail nobody needs to vary.
benefits: The consumer depends only on the abstraction it declares, so implementations vary without touching consuming code — the concrete choice is made once, at the edge of the application.
Testability: constructor injection lets a test hand in a fake, stub or spy directly, with no global state to reset, no module patched and no container started.
Dependencies become explicit in the API — constructor parameters, setters or injection interfaces state what the object needs — instead of hiding behind new, getInstance() or an import.
The whole graph can be validated and observed in one place, so missing bindings, unsatisfiable dependencies and cycles fail fast at start-up instead of at first use deep inside the code.
Lifetime and scope policy is centralised: the injector decides what is shared, what is per request and what is fresh per use, instead of every class caching its own singleton.
A composition root makes deployment variants first-class: production, sandbox, local and test configurations differ in a binding list rather than in conditional code paths.
Seams for cross-cutting concerns: decorators, proxies and middleware wrap injected services without modifying them.
Immutability is enforced: once a dependency is assigned to a constructor field it cannot be reassigned, eliminating an entire class of runtime bugs.
Refactoring safety: renaming or swapping a dependency requires only updating the composition root and tests, not every call site that constructs the class.
tradeoffs: Wiring moves into a second place: understanding an object graph now requires reading the binding configuration or composition root in addition to the classes themselves.
Unsatisfiable or ambiguous bindings are runtime failures unless the toolchain checks the graph at build time; a missing registration fails at start-up or, worse, at first use.
Container implementations that rely on reflection, proxies or generated metadata complicate stack traces, add start-up cost and make debugging less transparent.
Lifetime mistakes are the classic failure mode: a long-lived singleton that captures a request-scoped or transient dependency silently pins it for the process lifetime.

Constructor signatures grow with every new dependency, and the tempting escape hatch — injecting the container, a provider or a locator handle — reintroduces exactly the hidden dependencies the pattern removes.
Bindings and injection annotations or tokens couple code to a specific framework; migrating to another container or to plain hand-wiring means touching every declaration.
The bound implementation is not visible at the injection point: the interface hides the choice, so behaviour has to be traced into the configuration.
Setter and interface injection produce temporarily incomplete objects (a dependency can be forgotten or silently re-assigned), which is why constructor injection is the recommended default.
In functional programming contexts, DI makes functions impure — dependencies must be threading arguments rather than ambient state, complicating the type signatures.

participants.responsibility: Declares the collaborators it needs — as constructor parameters, setters/properties or an injection interface — and uses them, never constructing, locating or naming the concrete type itself.
The abstraction the consumer depends on; it is what makes the implementation swappable and keeps the dependency arrow pointing at a stable type. In hexagonal architecture this is called a 'port'.
The concrete class (or factory result) that satisfies the contract and is selected by configuration rather than by the consumer. In hexagonal architecture this is called an 'adapter'.
Resolves the graph from the bindings: constructs implementations, supplies their own dependencies recursively, applies the configured lifetime, and injects the result into the consumer.
The mapping from contract (or token) to implementation, factory or instance, together with its scope — expressed by annotations, a DSL/module, XML or plain registration code.

The single application location (main, bootstrapper, application factory, module) that selects concrete implementations, starts resolution and hands the assembled graph to the entry points; in hand-wired code it is the injector. Pure DI (no container) applies the same principle with manual constructor calls.

use_cases: Web and API backends whose handlers need repositories, clocks, mailers and caches that must be replaced by fakes in tests and by sandbox services in staging.
Hexagonal and clean architectures where the domain declares ports (interfaces) and the infrastructure layer supplies adapters at the composition root.
Frameworks that own object creation — request handlers, scheduled jobs, UI controllers, message consumers — where the framework's injector is the only practical wiring point.
Deployment variants (on-prem vs cloud, SQL vs in-memory, real vs stub payment gateway) selected per environment through binding configuration rather than conditional code.
Plugin and extension systems where the concrete implementation is chosen at start-up from a plugin registry, enabling third-party adapters without touching core code.
Expensive shared resources whose lifetime must be managed centrally (connection pools, HTTP clients, circuit breakers) while service classes stay stateless.
Unit tests that construct the class under test directly with test doubles, and integration tests that swap only the outer layer's bindings.
Microservices with sidecar containers: the sidecar provides logging, tracing and retry policies as injected collaborators, keeping the service logic untouched.
Cloud-native applications where the composition root is the only place that knows whether a dependency resolves locally, across a service mesh, or via a remote gRPC call.
Multi-tenant SaaS where tenant-specific adapters (tenant-scoped repositories, per-tenant feature flags) are bound at the composition root and switched by middleware.
Event-driven systems where message handlers receive their dependencies through injection, making the handler logic identical between in-process and distributed deployment.
AOT-compiled applications (Native AOT, Blazor WebAssembly, serverless) where runtime reflection is unavailable — dependencies are resolved via source generators or manually at the composition root.
Functional codebases using effect systems (ZIO, fp-ts, Reader monad) where the DI container is replaced by typed environments passed through function compositions.

Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI pact) where DI swaps provider implementations with contract-mock stubs at the boundary, enabling parallel service development without shared integration environments.

Resilience and fault-injection testing: proxies or decorator-based fault injectors (e.g., Gremlin SDK, WireMock) are injected as collaborators to validate retry, timeout and circuit-breaker behaviour under simulated failure conditions.

Single-page application frameworks with DI built into the component tree: Angular resolves components, directives and services through hierarchical injectors, scoping providers to the application root, a component subtree or a route so features override implementations and lazy-load without global registration.

Android apps using Dagger (and Hilt over it) to build the object graph at compile time — generated, reflection-free code, bindings and cycles checked at build time, with field injection reserved for framework-created entry points like Activities and Fragments.

Python web APIs (FastAPI) where each path operation declares Depends(callable) parameters: the framework resolves nested dependency graphs with per-request caching and uses yield-based dependencies to open and close connections around each request.
avoid_when: A small script, CLI or library function with one collaborator — constructing it inline is clearer than an injector plus a binding list.
The dependency is a value object or a pure computation — pass the value or call the function; an interface adds ceremony with no variability.
There is exactly one implementation and no test seam is needed — a plain constructor call in one place is simpler until a second implementation or a fake appears.
The objects are created and owned by a framework (entities, deserialization results, UI widgets built by the runtime) — only method or parameter injection at the boundary is possible there.
The environment cannot support the chosen realization (no runtime reflection and no build step to generate wiring) — hand-wired construction stays the fallback.
Pure functional code where the dependency graph can be expressed through function composition and partial application — explicit parameter passing eliminates the need for a container.
anti_patterns: Injecting the container, a provider or a locator handle instead of the collaborator — service-locator behaviour behind an injection-shaped signature.
Constructor injection used to pass data or parameters (request ids, configuration values) rather than services, turning the graph into a disguised parameter object.
Field injection into everything with the container as a global variable and no composition root, so no instance can be constructed without starting the container.
Reflection- or convention-driven wiring without start-up validation, so a typo in a binding surfaces at the first request.
Request- or task-scoped services captured by singletons (Captive Dependency) — silently leaks per-request state across all requests for the process lifetime.
An interface plus injection for every class 'just in case': one implementation, no seam, one more indirection to read.

Bastard Injection: providing default parameter values in constructors so the class can be instantiated without the container, undermining test control and making the dependency implicit rather than explicit.
Ambient Context: static or thread-local mutable state injected as a dependency, making tests order-sensitive and reintroducing hidden global state despite using DI.

Direct Container Call (DCC): application code explicitly calls the container's resolve API rather than accepting dependencies through constructors, coupling business logic to the container and hiding the dependency graph from static analysis.
Useless Injection: a dependency is declared in the constructor but never used inside the class; adds overhead, misleads readers and obscures the true dependency contract.
Intransigent Injection (IIJ): the container eagerly supplies a dependency the consumer does not need at construction time, causing unnecessary object construction and memory allocation.
Door Injection (ODI): the DI container or its API is passed as a dependency through layers of the application, coupling infrastructure concerns to domain code that should remain container-agnostic.
Fat DI Class (FDC): a consumer holds too many injected dependencies (typically more than 6-8), signalling that the class is doing too much and should be decomposed into smaller collaborators.
design_principles: Dependency Inversion Principle: depend on abstractions, not on concretions — the consumer names an interface it owns.
Inversion of Control: the assembler/framework calls you with your dependencies instead of your code reaching out for them.
Separation of construction from use: a class states what it needs; only the composition root knows how it is built.
Single Responsibility: declaring dependencies and building the graph are two responsibilities, held by the consumer and the root respectively.
Open/Closed: new implementations plug in through bindings, without edits to consumers.
Explicit Dependencies / Least Surprise: what an object needs is visible in its constructor, not hidden behind a lookup.
Interface Segregation: narrow interfaces per role prevent consumers from depending on unused operations; each consumer declares only the contracts it actually calls.
Explicit Dependencies Principle (ASP.NET Core): methods and classes should explicitly request their dependencies via constructors rather than relying on implicit service location.
Dependency Isolation Principle: a class should declare only the dependencies it actually invokes; unused injected dependencies constitute noise and indicate a potential design problem.
best_practices: Default to constructor injection with required dependencies as constructor parameters; use setter/property injection only for genuinely optional dependencies with sensible defaults; treat interface injection as a container-driven legacy form.
Keep one composition root per application (per entry point, per test) and keep all business logic out of it — it is a wiring-only zone.
Depend on interfaces owned by the consumer's layer (separated interface / ports), never on interfaces shipped with the implementation adapter.
Keep bindings in the outer infrastructure layer, declarative and grouped by feature; domain and application code must not reference the container.

Validate the entire graph at start-up: fail fast on missing or ambiguous bindings, detect cycles, and assert that scoped/transient dependencies are never injected into singletons where the container supports it. In .NET use ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild; in Java use @Validate on bean definition.
Enable scope validation in production builds — a misconfigured singleton capturing a scoped dependency silently leaks state across requests.
Choose the narrowest lifetime that is correct (transient → scoped → singleton); document each registration's lifetime and let the container dispose what it owns.

Never inject the container; inject the collaborators. If lazy construction is genuinely needed, inject a Factory<T> or a Provider<T>, not the service locator. The one legitimate exception is injecting IServiceScopeFactory into singletons that need scoped services — create an explicit scope per operation.
Treat a growing constructor (more than roughly four parameters) as a cohesion smell pointing at a missing abstraction — extract a parameters object or façade rather than switching to a locator.
Use the options pattern for configuration data (IOptions<T> / IConfiguration in .NET; @Value / @ConfigurationProperties in Spring) instead of injecting raw configuration sections as services.

When registering transient IDisposable services, ensure the container's lifetime model handles disposal — a transient capturing a scoped resource leaks it. Prefer the factory pattern so the consumer controls disposal timing.

Avoid ambient (global) mutable state injected as a dependency; prefer injecting ambient context providers that can be stubbed in tests without global mutation. If AsyncLocal<T> is used for request-scoped context, ensure the consumer is not singleton-registered.

For request-scoped data (user identity, tenant id, correlation id) that is infrastructural rather than domain behaviour, inject a IContextProvider<T> abstraction backed by AsyncLocal<T> rather than passing the raw value through constructors.
Treat DI container portability as a goal: prefer the standard (PSR-11, JSR-330, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection) over framework-specific attributes to keep migration paths open.

In functional codebases, declare dependencies as type parameters (Reader<E, A>, ZIO[R, E, A], ReaderTaskEither) and provide them via pure function composition rather than a runtime container — compile-time type checking replaces runtime resolution errors.
Use keyed services (AddKeyedService in .NET 8+, @Named in JSR-330) for multiple implementations of the same interface rather than overloading the single-abstract-member-per-interface rule.
For AOT-compatible applications, prefer source-generated DI (GenerateServiceProvider in .NET 8+, annotation processors in Java/Kotlin) over reflection-based containers that break trim analysis.

Prefer Pure DI (manual constructor wiring in the composition root) for applications with a stable, known-at-compile-time dependency graph — no runtime reflection, simpler debugging, no container magic.

Inject factories (IFactory<T>, Provider<T>, lazy<T>) instead of concrete async-initialised services to keep constructors synchronous; the factory encapsulates the async initialisation lifecycle without making the consumer's constructor async.

Register services close to their implementation: module-level registration files that live alongside the classes they register make the codebase easier to navigate and reduce the risk of forgotten or orphaned registrations.

Avoid assembly-scanning auto-registration without explicit fallback bindings — implicit resolution based on naming conventions hides the actual contract and breaks silently when a naming change occurs.
In integration tests, prefer a test-specific composition root over ad-hoc GetService calls on a shared container; each test gets a fresh graph so tests remain independent and order-insensitive.

Fowler, Inversion of Control (2005) | https://martinfowler.com/bliki/InversionOfControl.html | Distinguishes IoC as broad principle from DI as concrete form; explains Hollywood Principle.

Fowler, Refactoring Module Dependencies (2019) | https://martinfowler.com/articles/refactoring-dependencies.html | Refactoring from naive construction to Service Locator and then to Dependency Injection in Java and JavaScript; introduces the 'partial application for DI' approach in FP.

Seemann & van Deursen, Dependency Injection Principles, Practices, and Patterns (Manning, 2019) | https://www.manning.com/books/dependency-injection-principles-practices-and-patterns | Comprehensive reference covering DI lifetimes, composition root, pure DI, and container ecology; defines Captive Dependency anti-pattern.
JSR 330: Dependency Injection for Java (2009) | https://www.jcp.org/en/jsr/detail?id=330 | Standard annotation API: @Inject, @Named, @Singleton, Provider<T>; adopted by Guice, Spring, CDI.

Spring Framework Reference – Dependency Injection (2024) | https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/6.2/core/beans/dependencies/factory-collaborators.html | Constructor vs setter injection, bean scopes, circular dependency handling, nullability of injected beans.

.NET Dependency Injection Guidelines – Microsoft Learn (2024) | https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines | Service lifetimes, scope validation, disposable transients, options pattern, common misconfigurations, anti-patterns with concrete examples.

Microsoft – Service Lifetimes | https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-lifetimes | Detailed behaviour of transient, scoped and singleton lifetimes in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.

van Nieuwburg & Doolaard, Ambient Composition Model – Dotnet Junkie Blog | https://github.com/dotnetjunkie/blog/blob/master/content/posts/ambient-composition-model.md | Injecting ambient-context providers (AsyncLocal<T>) to keep domain objects stateless while preserving request-scoped context.

Remo Jansen, The Boundary Independence Principle (BIP) – DEV Community (2026) | https://dev.to/remojansen/the-boundary-independence-principle-bip-18me | Extends composition root to cross-process and remote boundaries; DI at the edge of the system rather than only at application start.

Microsoft Azure Architecture – Microservices Design Patterns | https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/patterns | Anti-Corruption Layer, Sidecar, BFF patterns in DI-heavy microservices.

Mark Seemann, Contravariant Dependency Injection (2022) | https://blog.ploeh.dk/2022/03/21/contravariant-dependency-injection/ | Explains why DI in FP is not 'just' a contravariant functor; DI makes functions impure regardless of how dependencies are passed.

ZIO Reference – Introduction to Dependency Injection in ZIO | https://zio.dev/reference/di/ | ZIO-native DI via ZEnvironment, ZLayer, ZIO.service and ZIO.provide; compile-time guarantee all dependencies are provided.

OOFP – Dependency Injection | https://oofp.js.org/guides/dependency-injection/ | Reader and ReaderTaskEither types for pure functional DI without containers in TypeScript/JavaScript; provide, provideRTE, chainwc patterns.

FunDI – Lightweight Dependency Injection for Functional Python (2026) | https://dev.to/kuyugama/fundi-lightweight-dependency-injection-for-functional-python-2dkm | Minimal functional DI library for Python; scope, from_, inject, lifespan dependencies without framework coupling.
Darky – ts-fp-di (TypeScript functional DI) | https://darky.github.io/ts-fp-di/ | TypeScript functional DI using AsyncLocalStorage; DI scope per HTTP request, di/diSet/diOnce API.

Autofac Documentation – Controlling Scope and Lifetime (2024) | https://autofac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/lifetime/ | Deep-dive into lifetime scopes, nesting, disposal tracking, and how singletons declared at different scope levels get their dependencies from different scopes.

Simple Injector – Lifetimes | https://docs.simpleinjector.org/en/latest/lifetimes.html | Transient lifestyle mismatch detection, scoped vs per-matching-lifetime, async disposal via DisposeAsync; transient-into-singleton is a compile-time warning.

Castle Windsor – Lifestyles | https://github.com/castleproject/Windsor/blob/master/docs/lifestyles.md | Singleton, transient, scoped lifestyles; CallContext scope for async flow; explicit Release required for manually resolved transients.

nWave – FP Hexagonal Architecture Skill (2026) | https://github.com/nWave-ai/nWave/blob/main/nWave/skills/nw-fp-hexagonal-architecture/SKILL.md | FP equivalents: ports as function signatures, adapters as concrete functions, DI via function parameters, Reader/environment pattern, effect systems.

DAP iQ – Dependency Injection Anti-Patterns in ASP.NET Core (2026) | https://dapiq.com/insights/dependency-injection-anti-patterns-aspnet-core | Five concrete anti-patterns: service locator, captive dependency, over-injection, disposable transients, lifetime mismatches, with detection strategies.

C# Corner – DI Done Right: Common Pitfalls (2026) | https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/blogs/dependency-injection-done-right-common-pitfalls-and-when-to-walk-away | Practical guidance on when not to use DI; avoiding configuration bloat, over-abstraction, and stateless utility injection.

George P. Wall – DI003 Captive Dependency Analyzer (2024) | https://georgepwall1991.github.io/DependencyInjection.Lifetime.Analyzers/rules/di003-captive-dependency/ | Defines all Captive Dependency paths including IEnumerable<T> collection captures, framework scoped services, and typed HttpClient registrations.

CodeWithMukesh – Transient, Scoped, Singleton in .NET (2025) | https://codewithmukesh.com/blog/when-to-use-transient-scoped-singleton-dotnet/ | Practical lifetime selection guide with .NET internals, disposal tracking, and IServiceScopeFactory patterns.

Arghajit & Bhopale et al., Cataloging Dependency Injection Anti-Patterns in Software Systems – arXiv:2109.04256 (2021, rev 2023) | https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2109.04256 | Peer-reviewed catalog of 12 DI anti-patterns (Intransigent Injection, Fat DI Class, Useless Injection, Direct Container Call, Door Injection, Bastard Injection, Captive Dependency, and others) with symptoms, root causes, consequences, and refactoring guidance; includes static analysis tool with 92% recall.

Mark Seemann, Service Locator: Roles vs. Mechanics – ploeh blog (2011) | https://blog.ploeh.dk/2011/08/25/ServiceLocatorrolesvs.mechanics/ | Clarifies that a DI container is not a Service Locator by its API shape alone; it becomes one only when application code queries it directly instead of receiving dependencies through constructors.

Mark Seemann, Composition Root – ploeh blog (2011) | https://blog.ploeh.dk/2011/07/28/CompositionRoot/ | Defines the Composition Root as the single location in an application where the object graph is assembled; libraries should not have one; each test method is a valid composition root.

arg.software – DI Anti-Patterns in ASP.NET Core (2024) | https://arg.software/blog/dependency-injection-anti-patterns-aspnet-core/ | Covers disposable transient memory leaks, scoped service captured by singleton, constructor over-injection, and the service locator pattern as the top DI mistakes in ASP.NET Core production code.

Angular Documentation – Dependency Injection | https://angular.dev/guide/di | Official DI guide: providers map tokens to values, hierarchical injectors mirror the component tree, and resolution walks element then environment injector hierarchies with route/module scoping.

Android Developers – Using Dagger in Android Apps | https://developer.android.com/training/dependency-injection/dagger-android | Official guidance for compile-time DI with Dagger: constructor injection by default, @Provides/@Binds modules, a scoped graph hosted by the Application class, field injection only for framework-instantiated Activities/Fragments.

FastAPI Documentation – Dependencies (FastAPI) | https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/ | Function-level DI: Depends() declares injectable callables, the framework resolves nested sub-dependency graphs with per-request caching and Annotated reusable dependencies, yield dependencies for teardown.

Nat Pryce, Dependency "Injection" Considered Harmful (2011) | http://www.natpryce.com/articles/000783.html | Critique of DI frameworks: dependencies should be explicit in an object's API and composition written as explicit code; frameworks that hide wiring behind reflection or XML obscure the design — containers justified mainly for dynamically loaded plug-ins.

Khalil Stemmler, Why I Don't Use a DI Container (2019) | https://khalilstemmler.com/articles/software-design-architecture/coding-without-di-container/ | Argues the ES module system plus feature-based packaging already gives composition and singletons; containers add noise, decorator clutter and circular-dependency risk, paying off only at large multi-team scale.
